Biography

Louisa Preston is a UK Space Agency Aurora research Fellow at Birkbeck, University of London, and a Lecturer in Space Science at NYU London. She has worked on projects for NASA and the Canadian, European and UK Space Agencies, and was on the science team for the PanCam instrument onboard the ExoMars 2020 rover. Louisa regularly works with the media, having appeared on many episodes of Sky at Night , BBC World Service , Fry and Rutherford and Women’s Hour . She has spoken at New Scientist Live, The Royal Institution, the Cheltenham Science Festival and The Lost Lectures, to name a few, and is a TED Fellow. She recently filmed a short documentary on her research for The Telegraph , and has consulted for many popular television science shows. She has penned articles for publications such as The Times , Wired , New Scientist and Vice . Her first book was Goldilocks and the Water Bears , which was published by Bloomsbury Sigma in 2016. @LouisaJPreston

BIO

Dr Louisa Preston is the Head of Planetary Science and Director of the Habitability Lab at UCL’s Mullard Space Science Laboratory (MSSL).

...

She is on the science team for the next European Space Agency Mars mission, the 2028 Rosalind Franklin Rover mission which will drill into the crust of Mars searching for signatures of buried ancient life. She is a Co-I for the PanCam instrument and a Co-I for the new Enfys spectrometer. Louisa is also a Co-I on the future Canadian Space Agency Lunar Rover Mission heading to the lunar south pole and is on the science team for the LAFORGE instrument.
Outside of academia, she is a science communicator and author, having written and contributed to four popular science books, including ‘Goldilocks and the Water Bears – The Search for Life in the Universe’ published by Bloomsbury.

As Goldilocks was searching for the perfect bowl of porridge, astrobiologists are searching for conditions throughout the Universe that are just right for life as we currently know it to exist.
With the Earth as our guide, the search has begun for similar worlds sitting at the perfect distance from their Sun – within the aptly named ‘Goldilocks Zone’ – that would enable them to keep water as a liquid on their surface and therefore perhaps support a thriving biosphere.
